## What it means

Git merges by walking both commit chains back to their **common ancestor**. That ancestor is what makes a merge a merge — Git uses it to decide which side changed what.

`refusing to merge unrelated histories` means Git found **no common ancestor at all**. The two histories are disjoint: neither side is a descendant of the other, and they don't share any commit. Git treats that as a mistake worth stopping on, because the usual causes are ones where a merge is not what you want.

## The usual causes

- You ran `git init` locally, made commits, then tried to `git pull` a remote that already has its own commits. Two independent root commits exist.
- A repo was re-created/re-initialized (fresh `git init`, new first commit) while the old clone or remote still has the original history.
- You're genuinely merging two separate projects that were never related (e.g. `git merge other-project`).

Before this got a flag (Git 2.9), the merge just happened silently and people got confused repos. The error is Git asking "are you sure?".

## The fixes, by intent

**You meant to join them** (e.g. adding a remote's history to your fresh local repo):

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

or for a local merge:

```
git merge --allow-unrelated-histories <branch>
```

This creates a merge commit whose history has **two roots**. It works, but every future merge and `git log` now carries two parallel histories — take it only when you really are combining two things.

**You didn't mean to have two histories** (the common case — e.g. you `git init`ed a directory that should have been a clone):

```
git remote add origin <url>      # if not set
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main     # discard local commits — they're gone
```

If you have local commits worth keeping, put them aside first (`git branch mine` or stash), reset to the remote, then `git cherry-pick` or re-apply them onto the real history. That keeps a single, linear ancestry instead of a two-root merge.

Which case you're in depends on whether your local commits are ones you want — the error itself doesn't tell you, so check `git log --oneline --graph --all` (and `git log --oneline origin/main`) to see what each side actually holds before picking.
